description: Question: if M 4.5 earthquakes happen every hour, how often does an M 8 happen, and which quakes release the Earth's seismic energy? Idea: the Gutenberg–Richter law, log₁₀ N(≥M) = a − bM: every magnitude unit is about ten times rarer (b ≈ 1). USGS's FDSN event service gives every M ≥ 4.5 earthquake worldwide in 2025 (about 8,560). Polars bins them at 0.1, finds the completeness magnitude by maximum curvature (Mc = 4.7) and estimates b by Aki–Utsu maximum likelihood with Shi–Bolt's standard error: b = 1.15 ± 0.02 (4,728 quakes ≥ 4.7) for the mixed catalogue, so the law predicts 12 M 7+ a year (16 occurred) and an M 8+ every 14 months or so (one occurred). The b-value against Mc shows a catch: small quakes are reported in body-wave mb, large ones in moment magnitude Mw, so each family alone is cut off at one end; Mw's b settles near 1 (0.99 at Mc 5.5) once Mc is past its cut. A catalogue's b depends on its magnitude scale. With energy ∝ 10^(1.5M), the counts fall tenfold per unit while energy per bin grows: in 2025 the M 8.8 Kamchatka earthquake alone released about 83% of the year's seismic energy. Caveats: magnitudes mix mb, Mww and others; the global M 4.5 floor is incomplete in places (oceans, poorly instrumented regions) above 4.5; aftershocks are not removed (declustering changes b a little); one year is a short window for M 8 rates. Next: b per region or depth (table), b before and after a large quake, or the Omori law of its aftershocks (the same service, a circle around the epicentre).
name: The Gutenberg–Richter law and the b-value
